o: Count index quadruplets i<j<k<l with nums[i]<nums[k]<nums[j]<nums[l], where nums is a permutation of 1..n with n up to 4000. An O(n⁴) or even O(n³) scan is too slow (~10¹¹–10¹³ ops), so we must fix the middle pair (j,k) and count valid i and l in aggregate. In Example 1 the two quadruplets share i=0, j=1, k=2 and differ only in l.
k: Fix the middle pair (j,k); the conditions on i and l decouple.
A(j,k) = #{i<j: nums[i]<nums[k]} and B(j,k) = #{l>k: nums[l]>nums[j]} can both be maintained with running counts.
Answer = Σ over j<k with nums[k]<nums[j] of A(j,k)·B(j,k).

a.n: Approach 1: Rolling counts over the middle pair — O(n²) time, O(n) space
a.i: Iterate j from right to left. Maintain lessBefore[k] = how many indices i < j have nums[i] < nums[k]: each time we finish a j, element nums[j] joins the 'before' set, incrementing lessBefore[k] for every k with nums[k] > nums[j] — an O(n) bulk update, no BIT needed. For the same j, scan k from right to left keeping great = #{l>k: nums[l]>nums[j]}; whenever nums[k] < nums[j] we add lessBefore[k]·great to the answer.
s: For j from n−1 down to 0: scan k from n−1 down to j+1, adding lessBefore[k]·great when nums[k]<nums[j] and incrementing great when nums[k]>nums[j].
Then extend the 'before' set with element j: for all k, if nums[k]>nums[j], increment lessBefore[k].
a.t: O(n²) — for each j, two linear scans over the array (~16M operations at n=4000)

a.i: The same formula can be implemented more literally: precompute lt[j][k] = #{i<j: nums[i]<nums[k]} row by row (each row extends the previous by one element) and gt[j][k] = #{l>k: nums[l]>nums[j]}, then sum products over all pairs j<k with nums[k]<nums[j]. This is easier to reason about but uses Θ(n²) memory (~tens of MB at n=4000), which is riskier.
s: Build lt row by row: lt[j] = lt[j−1] shifted by including element j−1.
Build gt row by row from the right.
Accumulate lt[j][k]·gt[j][k] over pairs with nums[k]<nums[j].
a.sp: O(n²) — two n×n tables dominate memory

w: Present Approach 1 in an interview; mention that a Fenwick tree gives the same counts in O(n² log n) if the bulk-update trick is not spotted. Pitfalls: off-by-one on whether i=j is allowed (it is not — hence the update happens after the k-scan), and overflow (use 64-bit accumulation; the answer can exceed 10⁹).
